message.content: Read redu.md and deploy Formbricks on redu.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- investigate: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. (gstack)
- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.content:
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/formbricks/formbricks
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/formbricks/formbricks:5.3.4
  port: 3000
  vm: m1.mem16
  flavor_id: "7"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2", db_extensions pgvector)
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.073
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: formbricks
quirks:
  - "⛔ SAY THIS BEFORE THE PLAN IS APPROVED: THIS ONE IS NOT IN THE NO-CARD FREE TRIAL. The trial ceiling is an m1.medium VM plus one m1.small managed database. This recipe asks for m1.mem16 because the v5 baseline runs five long-running containers, so it needs a card. About GBP 0.073/hr, roughly GBP 53 a month. Tell the user that up front rather than letting them discover it as a quota rejection after they have said yes."
  - "⛔⛔ THE FIRST PERSON TO REACH /setup/signup BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR OF THE WHOLE INSTANCE. Verified: apps/web/modules/auth/signup/actions.ts:356-371 allows an uninvited sign-up only when getIsFreshInstance() is true, and apps/web/lib/instance/service.ts defines fresh as prisma.user.count() === 0. The page itself (modules/setup/(fresh-instance)/signup/page.tsx) is headed \"Create administrator\" and \"This user has all the power\". It is unauthenticated by design. So from the moment the container serves until somebody signs up, the instance belongs to whoever loads that URL. CLAIM IT IMMEDIATELY, as part of the deploy, before you hand the hostname to anybody. This is a BROWSER step: sign-up is a Next.js server action, not a documented REST endpoint, so do not try to script it with curl. Then run the verification script in the body of this file, which proves the window is shut."
  - "✅ AND THEN IT CLOSES ITSELF, PERMANENTLY, WITH NO SETTING TO REMEMBER. Once one user row exists the instance is no longer fresh, and apps/web/lib/constants.ts:66 defines SIGNUP_ENABLED as IS_FORMBRICKS_CLOUD || IS_DEVELOPMENT || E2E_TESTING, none of which is true on a self-hosted production build. Public sign-up is therefore hardcoded OFF and new users can only arrive by invitation. The route disappears too: modules/setup/(fresh-instance)/layout.tsx calls notFound() once the instance is not fresh, so a 404 on /setup/signup is the POSITIVE result and a 200 there is the failure. Get that polarity the right way round in any check you write."
  - "⛔ THERE IS NO SIGNUP_DISABLED VARIABLE IN 5.3.4, AND SETTING ONE DOES NOTHING. Tutorials and older self-hosting posts tell you to set SIGNUP_DISABLED=1. apps/web/lib/env.ts has no such key and constants.ts:66 derives SIGNUP_ENABLED without reading the environment at all, so the variable is inert. Do not report an instance as locked down because you set it. The thing that actually closes the door is a user existing. INVITE_DISABLED=1 is real (constants.ts:68) and turns off invitations too, which is a different and much stronger decision to make with the user."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH. The management app requires a session. What is public BY DESIGN is the survey surface: a link survey at /s/<surveyId> is meant to be answered by strangers, and that is the product working, not a leak. Also anonymous: /auth/login, /health (a static {\"status\":\"ok\"}), /api/v2/health, and, until it is claimed, /setup/signup. Nothing else. Say this to the user plainly, because \"my survey tool is publicly reachable\" sounds alarming and is the entire point."
  - "⛔⛔ DO NOT LET ANY SERVICE ASK FOR A SECOND DATABASE. This is redu's sharpest platform trap and Formbricks walks straight into it: .env.example:67 sets HUB_DATABASE_URL to postgresql://.../hub, a SECOND database named hub on the same server. A redu managed Postgres scopes its pg_hba.conf to the ONE database it provisioned, so any other database on that server is refused at AUTHENTICATION, SQLSTATE 28000, before privileges are consulted, and being superuser does not help. It broke two of the first eleven entries in this library and both looked healthy. The fix is already upstream's production default: LEAVE HUB_DATABASE_URL UNSET, or set it to exactly the same value as DATABASE_URL, so Hub, Cube and the web app all share one database. docker/docker-compose.yml says so in its own comment: \"Default: same Postgres as Formbricks. Set only if Hub uses a separate DB.\" Ignore .env.example on this point."
  - "PASS db_extensions pgvector WHEN YOU CREATE THE DATABASE. packages/database/schema/main.prisma:6,12 declares extensions = [pgvector(map: \"vector\")], and upstream's compose deliberately pins pgvector/pgvector:pg18 instead of a plain postgres image. No migration in the repository was found actually creating the extension, so this is a PRECAUTION rather than a proven requirement, and it is a free one: deploy_compose takes db_extensions: ['pgvector'] and redu installs it at provision time. A missing extension shows up as a FAILED MIGRATION at boot, not as a runtime error, so it is cheap to prevent and annoying to diagnose."
  - "⚠️ REDU'S MANAGED POSTGRES IS 16, 15 OR 14 (DEFAULT 16). UPSTREAM SHIPS 18. Nothing read in this repository requires 18, and a Prisma-plus-goose migration set is normally version-agnostic, but this is UNVERIFIED and it is the first thing to check if formbricks-migrate or hub-migrate fails on syntax. Do not report it as fine because the app came up: the migration jobs run before the app does."
  - "THE THREE SECRETS THAT MUST BE SET EXPLICITLY AND REUSED ON EVERY REDEPLOY. ENCRYPTION_KEY is required at startup (apps/web/lib/env.ts:238) and encrypts two-factor secrets and single-use link-survey URLs: change it and those stop decrypting. NEXTAUTH_SECRET signs sessions: change it and everyone is signed out. CUBEJS_API_SECRET signs the JWTs the web app uses to call Cube, and Cube's own entrypoint EXITS if it is empty. HUB_API_KEY is required too (env.ts:273). Generate all four as long alphanumeric values, record them wherever the user keeps deploy secrets, and pass the SAME ones next time. None of them is recoverable from the running system."
  - "DATABASE WIRING, AND CUBE IS THE ONE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE. redu injects DATABASE_URL plus PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, PGUSER and PGPASSWORD into the project .env, and deploy_compose NEVER edits your compose, so every service must interpolate them itself. The web app, its migration job and Hub all read DATABASE_URL. CUBE DOES NOT: it reads CUBEJS_DB_HOST, CUBEJS_DB_PORT, CUBEJS_DB_NAME, CUBEJS_DB_USER and CUBEJS_DB_PASS as five separate values, so map them from the PG* variables by hand. Note CUBEJS_DB_PASS, not CUBEJS_DB_PASSWORD, and CUBEJS_DB_NAME, not CUBEJS_DB_DATABASE. If Hub's Go client rejects the connection on TLS, append ?sslmode=disable to ITS url only, which is what upstream's own default does."
  - "⛔ CUBE BIND-MOUNTS TWO FILES THAT ARE NOT IN ANY IMAGE, AND WITHOUT THEM NOTHING STARTS. The cube service mounts ./cube/cube.js and ./cube/schema read-only. They live in the REPO at docker/cube/cube.js and docker/cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js and are not baked into cubejs/cube. Because this is an upload deploy, they will simply be missing unless you put them in the tarball: fetch both from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag 5.3.4 into cube/cube.js and cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js beside your compose. Their absence is not a quiet degradation: Cube fails its /readyz healthcheck, the formbricks service waits on cube being healthy, and the hostname answers 502 forever with no obvious cause. docker.mdx:586 lists exactly this as the reason Cube is unhealthy."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE ports BLOCK FROM THE REDIS SERVICE. Upstream's production compose publishes Valkey on host port 6379 and sets no password on it. That is a local-development convenience sitting in a file labelled production. Formbricks reaches Valkey over the compose network as redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password] nothing needs it on the host. Publish ONLY the web app's 3000."
  - "DELETE THE BUNDLED postgres SERVICE, AND THEN DELETE ITS depends_on ENTRIES TOO. This is the step people half-do. Removing the postgres service while leaving a depends_on entry naming postgres with condition service_healthy on formbricks, formbricks-migrate, hub or cube makes compose refuse the whole file with an undefined-service error, which reads like a syntax problem rather than the leftover it is. Keep the redis and cube depends_on conditions; drop every postgres one."
  - "PIN BOTH IMAGES, AND PIN THEM AS A PAIR. Upstream's production compose uses :latest for the web image and for Hub, which is not something to hand a stranger. Use ghcr.io/formbricks/formbricks:5.3.4 and ghcr.io/formbricks/hub:0.8.4; docker-compose.dev.yml:146 defaults HUB_IMAGE_TAG to 0.8.4, which is the evidence that this is the Hub release paired with the 5.3.x web app. Cube is already pinned upstream at cubejs/cube:v1.6.6 and Valkey by digest; keep both exactly as upstream has them. Hub's migrations run against the shared database, so a mismatched Hub version is a schema question, not a cosmetic one."
  - "SKIP THE OPTIONAL PROFILES. The compose carries two profiles that are off by default and must stay off: taxonomy (an AI classification service) and qwen, which requests an NVIDIA GPU in its deploy.resources block. redu VMs have no GPU, so enabling qwen produces a container that cannot schedule. RustFS and S3 storage are also optional; without them, file uploads land on the app VM's disk."
  - "THE PUBLIC URL MUST BE KNOWN BEFORE THE CONTAINER STARTS. WEBAPP_URL and NEXTAUTH_URL both need the final https:// address, and Next.js bakes URL-derived behaviour at boot rather than discovering it from the Host header. Generate the dname yourself in full formbricks-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form, set both variables to https://<that>, and pass the same name to deploy_compose. Getting this wrong presents as broken redirects and links after sign-in, not as a startup error."
  - "USE A NAMED VOLUME FOR /home/nextjs/apps/web/saml-connection, NOT UPSTREAM'S BIND MOUNT. apps/web/Dockerfile:335,338 creates that directory and declares it a VOLUME, and the app runs as the non-root user nextjs (:331). A host bind mount to a path that does not exist yet is created by Docker owned by root, which the app then cannot write. A NAMED volume is seeded from the image on first use, ownership included. SAML is an enterprise feature most self-hosters never touch, but the path still has to be writable."
  - "MIGRATIONS ARE TWO SEPARATE ONE-SHOT JOBS AND THEY ARE ORDERED. formbricks-migrate runs the web app's Prisma migrations; hub-migrate then runs goose plus river for Hub, into the SAME database, and only starts after the first has completed successfully. The long-running formbricks service is started with SKIP_STARTUP_MIGRATION set to true precisely so it does not race them. Keep the ordering, and read BOTH jobs' logs before concluding a boot failure is the app's fault."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO RAM FIGURE. Checked the README, the compose files, apps/web/Dockerfile and the self-hosting docs: no memory number. m1.mem16 (4 vCPU / 16 GB) follows the precedent this library set for a multi-container stack and is reasoning from a Next.js server, a Cube.js server with an in-memory cache and queue driver, a Go API and a Valkey sharing one box. It may well be generous: if a real run shows it fits comfortably in m1.medium, that would move this entry INSIDE the free trial, which is worth the measurement. Write the number back rather than repeating this paragraph."
  - "⚠️ plan_deploy WILL QUOTE m1.large ONCE needs_compose IS DECLARED, and here that is a DOWNGRADE, not an upsell: m1.large is 4 vCPU / 8 GB while m1.mem16 is 4 vCPU / 16 GB for GBP 0.007 more per hour. # Self-host Formbricks on redu

Your own experience management and survey platform, in the EU, on infrastructure you control: the
Formbricks v5 baseline stack on one VM, with a managed Postgres beside it that survives every
redeploy.

## What this deploys

- **Formbricks web** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.mem16 VM, port 3000.
- **Formbricks Hub** and **Cube**, which are part of the v5 baseline and not optional.
- **Valkey** for caching, rate limiting and audit logging, on a named volume.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, with the pgvector extension pre-installed.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month.

⚠️ **This one does not fit the no-card free trial.** The trial caps a VM at m1.medium and one
managed database at m1.small; this stack asks for m1.mem16. That is worth knowing before you start,
not after a quota rejection.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Formbricks on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Claim the administrator account, immediately

The moment the hostname answers, open:

    https://<your-host>/setup/signup

The page is headed **"Create administrator"** and, underneath, **"This user has all the power"**.
It is unauthenticated on purpose, because a fresh instance has nobody to authenticate. Whoever
fills it in first owns the instance.

There is no way to close that window with a setting, and no bootstrap token. The only thing that
closes it is claiming the account. So claim it as part of the deploy, before the URL goes anywhere.

**Then it shuts by itself and stays shut.** Once one user exists the instance is no longer
"fresh": public sign-up is compiled off for self-hosted builds, the setup route stops existing, and
new people can only arrive by invitation. Nothing to configure, nothing to remember.

Sign-up is a Next.js server action rather than a REST endpoint, so this step is a browser step. Do
not try to curl it. Verify the outcome instead, with the script below.

## The four that actually break it

**A second database.** Formbricks' own `.env.example` points Hub at a separate database called
`hub`. A redu managed Postgres serves exactly one database and refuses every other one at
authentication, superuser or not. Leave `HUB_DATABASE_URL` unset so Hub shares the app's
database, which is what upstream's production compose does anyway.

**Cube's two config files.** The Cube service bind-mounts `./cube/cube.js` and `./cube/schema`
from the repository. They are not in any published image. Missing, Cube never becomes healthy, the
web app waits on it forever, and the hostname answers 502 with nothing in the app's log to explain
it.

**Valkey published on the host.** Upstream's production compose maps `6379:6379` and sets no
password. Delete that `ports:` block; the app reaches it over the compose network.

**The leftover `depends_on`.** Deleting the bundled `postgres` service without also deleting
every `depends_on: postgres` makes compose reject the file outright, which reads like a syntax
error rather than the half-finished edit it is.

## The compose

Five services, plus two one-shot migration jobs, with the bundled Postgres replaced by redu's
managed one:

```yaml

  CUBEJS_API_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"

  CUBEJS_JWT_AUDIENCE: "formbricks-cube"

services:
  redis:
    image: valkey/valkey@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:2e96e9e9»
    restart: always
    command: valkey-server --appendonly yes --maxmemory-policy noeviction
    volumes:
      - redis:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "valkey-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30

  formbricks-migrate:
    image: ghcr.io/formbricks/formbricks:5.3.4
    restart: "no"

    environment:

    depends_on:

  hub:

    depends_on:
      hub-migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  cube:
    image: cubejs/cube:v1.6.6
    restart: always
    environment:
      CUBEJS_DB_TYPE: postgres
      CUBEJS_DB_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
      CUBEJS_DB_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
      CUBEJS_DB_NAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
      CUBEJS_DB_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      CUBEJS_DB_PASS: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      CUBEJS_API_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      CUBEJS_JWT_ISSUER: "formbricks-web"
      CUBEJS_JWT_AUDIENCE: "formbricks-cube"
      CUBEJS_DEFAULT_API_SCOPES: meta,data
      CUBEJS_CACHE_AND_QUEUE_DRIVER: memory
    volumes:
      - ./cube/cube.js:/cube/conf/cube.js:ro
      - ./cube/schema:/cube/conf/model:ro
    depends_on:
      hub-migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "node", "-e", "require('http').get('http://127.0.0.1:4000/readyz', (r) => process.exit(r.statusCode === 200 ? 0 : 1)).on('error', () => process.exit(1));"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 30s

    image: ghcr.io/formbricks/formbricks:5.3.4
    restart: always
    environment:
      <<: *app-env
      SKIP_STARTUP_MIGRATION: "true"
    volumes:
      - saml:/home/nextjs/apps/web/saml-connection
    ports:

    depends_on:

  saml:
```

Fetch Cube's two config files into the same directory before uploading:

```bash
mkdir -p cube/schema
curl -fsSL -o cube/cube.js \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/formbricks/formbricks/5.3.4/docker/cube/cube.js
curl -fsSL -o cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/formbricks/formbricks/5.3.4/docker/cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js
test -s cube/cube.js && test -s cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js \
  || { echo "Cube config missing; the stack will never become healthy" >&2; exit 1; }
```

## Verify it: reached the database, and the setup door is shut

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Formbricks reached its managed database and that nobody else can claim it.
#   ./verify.sh formbricks-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = pass, 1 = FAIL (act now), 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE, and pick the endpoint that proves the most. /health is a static {"status":"ok"} and
#    tells you nothing about the database. /api/v2/health queries Postgres AND pings Redis, so a
#    200 here proves the whole data path, not just that Next.js is listening.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v2/health")
case "$code" in
  200) echo "OK: app, managed Postgres and Valkey are all answering." ;;
  502)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from redu's proxy. The container is still starting; wait and re-run." >&2
    echo "  If it STAYS 502, suspect Cube: the web app waits on cube being healthy, and Cube" >&2
    echo "  never becomes healthy without cube/cube.js and cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js." >&2
    exit 2 ;;
  503)
    echo "FAIL: the health check ran and reported a dependency DOWN (HTTP 503)." >&2
    echo "  That is the database or the cache, not the web app. Read formbricks-migrate and" >&2
    echo "  hub-migrate logs first; a second database named 'hub' fails here with SQLSTATE 28000." >&2
    cat "$TMP/health" >&2
    exit 1 ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v2/health answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
    exit 2 ;;
esac

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Prove it is Formbricks on this hostname and not something else, so that
#    the negative assertion below cannot pass vacuously against an error page.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/auth/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -qi 'formbricks' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /auth/login answered HTTP $code without identifying as Formbricks." >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: the login page is served by Formbricks."

# 3. THE ASSERTION, and mind the polarity: the setup route is REMOVED once a user exists, so
#    404 (or a redirect to the login page) is the PASS and 200 is the failure. Do not follow
#    redirects here, or a 302 to /auth/login arrives as a 200 and reads as OPEN.
code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/signup")
case "$code" in
  200)
    echo "FAIL: /setup/signup is STILL SERVING. This instance has no administrator and the next" >&2
    echo "  person to load that page becomes it, with all the power. Claim it in a browser NOW." >&2
    exit 1 ;;
  404|301|302|303|307|308)
    echo "OK: /setup/signup answers $code, so an administrator exists and the route is gone." ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup/signup answered HTTP $code, which this check does not understand." >&2
    echo "  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of an unrecognised code." >&2
    exit 2 ;;
esac

echo
echo "PASS: [REDACTED:value] path healthy, administrator claimed, setup route closed."
```

And on the VM itself, once it is up:

```bash
# Note redu's VMs run docker, not podman: a missing command prints an error and greps to zero
# matches, which reads as a pass. So check the positive half too.
sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'          # expect formbricks, hub, cube, redis
sudo docker ps -a --filter 'name=migrate' --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'  # both Exited (0)

C=$(sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -E 'formbricks(-|_)[0-9]|formbricks$' | head -n1)
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "no formbricks container found; nothing below means anything" >&2; exit 1; }

# Positive half: the app is pointed at the PRIVATE database VM, not at something in the compose.
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv DATABASE_URL | sed 's|//[^@]*@|//<redacted>@|'

# Negative half: no service is asking for a second database. Anything here is the 28000 trap.
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv HUB_DATABASE_URL && echo "^^ UNSET THIS" || echo "OK: HUB_DATABASE_URL is unset"
```

# Self-host Formbricks on redu

Your own experience management and survey platform, in the EU, on infrastructure you control: the
Formbricks v5 baseline stack on one VM, with a managed Postgres beside it that survives every
redeploy.

## What this deploys

- **Formbricks web** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.mem16 VM, port 3000.
- **Formbricks Hub** and **Cube**, which are part of the v5 baseline and not optional.
- **Valkey** for caching, rate limiting and audit logging, on a named volume.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, with the pgvector extension pre-installed.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month.

⚠️ **This one does not fit the no-card free trial.** The trial caps a VM at m1.medium and one
managed database at m1.small; this stack asks for m1.mem16. That is worth knowing before you start,
not after a quota rejection.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Formbricks on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Claim the administrator account, immediately

The moment the hostname answers, open:

    https://<your-host>/setup/signup

The page is headed **"Create administrator"** and, underneath, **"This user has all the power"**.
It is unauthenticated on purpose, because a fresh instance has nobody to authenticate. Whoever
fills it in first owns the instance.

There is no way to close that window with a setting, and no bootstrap token. The only thing that
closes it is claiming the account. So claim it as part of the deploy, before the URL goes anywhere.

**Then it shuts by itself and stays shut.** Once one user exists the instance is no longer
"fresh": public sign-up is compiled off for self-hosted builds, the setup route stops existing, and
new people can only arrive by invitation. Nothing to configure, nothing to remember.

Sign-up is a Next.js server action rather than a REST endpoint, so this step is a browser step. Do
not try to curl it. Verify the outcome instead, with the script below.

## The four that actually break it

**A second database.** Formbricks' own `.env.example` points Hub at a separate database called
`hub`. A redu managed Postgres serves exactly one database and refuses every other one at
authentication, superuser or not. Leave `HUB_DATABASE_URL` unset so Hub shares the app's
database, which is what upstream's production compose does anyway.

**Cube's two config files.** The Cube service bind-mounts `./cube/cube.js` and `./cube/schema`
from the repository. They are not in any published image. Missing, Cube never becomes healthy, the
web app waits on it forever, and the hostname answers 502 with nothing in the app's log to explain
it.

**Valkey published on the host.** Upstream's production compose maps `6379:6379` and sets no
password. Delete that `ports:` block; the app reaches it over the compose network.

**The leftover `depends_on`.** Deleting the bundled `postgres` service without also deleting
every `depends_on: postgres` makes compose reject the file outright, which reads like a syntax
error rather than the half-finished edit it is.

## The compose

Five services, plus two one-shot migration jobs, with the bundled Postgres replaced by redu's
managed one:

```yaml
x-app-env: &app-env
  WEBAPP_URL: "https://${FB_HOST}"
  NEXTAUTH_URL: "https://${FB_HOST}"
  DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
  ENCRYPTION_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
  NEXTAUTH_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
  CRON_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
  REDIS_URL: "redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password]"
  HUB_API_URL: "http://hub:8080"
  HUB_API_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
  CUBEJS_API_URL: "http://cube:4000"
  CUBEJS_API_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
  CUBEJS_JWT_ISSUER: "formbricks-web"
  CUBEJS_JWT_AUDIENCE: "formbricks-cube"
  EMAIL_VERIFICATION_DISABLED: "1"
  PASSWORD_RESET_DISABLED: "1"

services:
  redis:
    image: valkey/valkey@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:2e96e9e9»
    restart: always
    command: valkey-server --appendonly yes --maxmemory-policy noeviction
    volumes:
      - redis:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "valkey-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30

  formbricks-migrate:
    image: ghcr.io/formbricks/formbricks:5.3.4
    restart: "no"
    entrypoint: ["sh", "-c"]
    command:
      - "node /home/nextjs/validate-env.mjs && node packages/database/dist/scripts/apply-migrations.js"
    environment: *app-env

  hub-migrate:
    image: ghcr.io/formbricks/hub:0.8.4
    restart: "no"
    entrypoint: ["sh", "-c"]
    command:
      - '/usr/local/bin/goose -dir /app/migrations postgres "$$DATABASE_URL" up && /usr/local/bin/river migrate-up --database-url "$$DATABASE_URL"'
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
    depends_on:
      formbricks-migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  hub:
    image: ghcr.io/formbricks/hub:0.8.4
    restart: always
    environment:
      API_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
    depends_on:
      hub-migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  cube:
    image: cubejs/cube:v1.6.6
    restart: always
    environment:
      CUBEJS_DB_TYPE: postgres
      CUBEJS_DB_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
      CUBEJS_DB_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
      CUBEJS_DB_NAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
      CUBEJS_DB_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      CUBEJS_DB_PASS: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      CUBEJS_API_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      CUBEJS_JWT_ISSUER: "formbricks-web"
      CUBEJS_JWT_AUDIENCE: "formbricks-cube"
      CUBEJS_DEFAULT_API_SCOPES: meta,data
      CUBEJS_CACHE_AND_QUEUE_DRIVER: memory
    volumes:
      - ./cube/cube.js:/cube/conf/cube.js:ro
      - ./cube/schema:/cube/conf/model:ro
    depends_on:
      hub-migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "node", "-e", "require('http').get('http://127.0.0.1:4000/readyz', (r) => process.exit(r.statusCode === 200 ? 0 : 1)).on('error', () => process.exit(1));"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 30s

  formbricks:
    image: ghcr.io/formbricks/formbricks:5.3.4
    restart: always
    environment:
      <<: *app-env
      SKIP_STARTUP_MIGRATION: "true"
    volumes:
      - saml:/home/nextjs/apps/web/saml-connection
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      cube:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  redis:
  saml:
```

Fetch Cube's two config files into the same directory before uploading:

```bash
mkdir -p cube/schema
curl -fsSL -o cube/cube.js \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/formbricks/formbricks/5.3.4/docker/cube/cube.js
curl -fsSL -o cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/formbricks/formbricks/5.3.4/docker/cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js
test -s cube/cube.js && test -s cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js \
  || { echo "Cube config missing; the stack will never become healthy" >&2; exit 1; }
```

## Verify it: reached the database, and the setup door is shut

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Formbricks reached its managed database and that nobody else can claim it.
#   ./verify.sh formbricks-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = pass, 1 = FAIL (act now), 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE, and pick the endpoint that proves the most. /health is a static {"status":"ok"} and
#    tells you nothing about the database. /api/v2/health queries Postgres AND pings Redis, so a
#    200 here proves the whole data path, not just that Next.js is listening.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v2/health")
case "$code" in
  200) echo "OK: app, managed Postgres and Valkey are all answering." ;;
  502)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from redu's proxy. The container is still starting; wait and re-run." >&2
    echo "  If it STAYS 502, suspect Cube: the web app waits on cube being healthy, and Cube" >&2
    echo "  never becomes healthy without cube/cube.js and cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js." >&2
    exit 2 ;;
  503)
    echo "FAIL: the health check ran and reported a dependency DOWN (HTTP 503)." >&2
    echo "  That is the database or the cache, not the web app. Read formbricks-migrate and" >&2
    echo "  hub-migrate logs first; a second database named 'hub' fails here with SQLSTATE 28000." >&2
    cat "$TMP/health" >&2
    exit 1 ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v2/health answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
    exit 2 ;;
esac

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Prove it is Formbricks on this hostname and not something else, so that
#    the negative assertion below cannot pass vacuously against an error page.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/auth/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -qi 'formbricks' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /auth/login answered HTTP $code without identifying as Formbricks." >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: the login page is served by Formbricks."

# 3. THE ASSERTION, and mind the polarity: the setup route is REMOVED once a user exists, so
#    404 (or a redirect to the login page) is the PASS and 200 is the failure. Do not follow
#    redirects here, or a 302 to /auth/login arrives as a 200 and reads as OPEN.
code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup/signup")
case "$code" in
  200)
    echo "FAIL: /setup/signup is STILL SERVING. This instance has no administrator and the next" >&2
    echo "  person to load that page becomes it, with all the power. Claim it in a browser NOW." >&2
    exit 1 ;;
  404|301|302|303|307|308)
    echo "OK: /setup/signup answers $code, so an administrator exists and the route is gone." ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup/signup answered HTTP $code, which this check does not understand." >&2
    echo "  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of an unrecognised code." >&2
    exit 2 ;;
esac

echo
echo "PASS: [REDACTED:value] path healthy, administrator claimed, setup route closed."
```

And on the VM itself, once it is up:

```bash
# Note redu's VMs run docker, not podman: a missing command prints an error and greps to zero
# matches, which reads as a pass. So check the positive half too.
sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'          # expect formbricks, hub, cube, redis
sudo docker ps -a --filter 'name=migrate' --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'  # both Exited (0)

C=$(sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -E 'formbricks(-|_)[0-9]|formbricks$' | head -n1)
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "no formbricks container found; nothing below means anything" >&2; exit 1; }

# Positive half: the app is pointed at the PRIVATE database VM, not at something in the compose.
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv DATABASE_URL | sed 's|//[^@]*@|//<redacted>@|'

# Negative half: no service is asking for a second database. Anything here is the 28000 trap.
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv HUB_DATABASE_URL && echo "^^ UNSET THIS" || echo "OK: HUB_DATABASE_URL is unset"
```

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. quirks:
  - "NOT IN THE NO-CARD FREE TRIAL. m1.mem16 required for five long-running containers. About GBP 0.073/hr."
  - "FIRST PERSON TO REACH /setup/signup BECOMES ADMINISTRATOR. Claim immediately in a browser; it is a Next.js server action, not curl-able."
  - "Once one user row exists the route 404s permanently. SIGNUP_ENABLED is hardcoded off for self-hosted."
  - "NO SIGNUP_DISABLED VARIABLE EXISTS IN 5.3.4; setting it does nothing."
  - "DO NOT LET ANY SERVICE ASK FOR A SECOND DATABASE. Leave HUB_DATABASE_URL UNSET (redu managed PG refuses other DBs with SQLSTATE 28000)."
  - "PASS db_extensions pgvector AT CREATE TIME (main.prisma declares the extension)."
  - "CUBE reads CUBEJS_DB_HOST/PORT/NAME/USER/PASS, not DATABASE_URL. Map from PG* by hand."
  - "CUBE BIND-MOUNTS ./cube/cube.js AND ./cube/schema WHICH ARE NOT IN ANY IMAGE. Fetch from raw.githubusercontent at 5.3.4 into the tarball or the stack 502s forever."

  - "PIN ghcr.io/formbricks/formbricks:5.3.4 WITH ghcr.io/formbricks/hub:0.8.4 as a pair."
  - "SKIP the taxonomy and qwen profiles (qwen needs an NVIDIA GPU)."
  - "WEBAPP_URL and NEXTAUTH_URL must be the final https URL before boot; generate the full dname yourself."
  - "USE A NAMED VOLUME for /home/nextjs/apps/web/saml-connection, not a bind mount."
  - "MIGRATIONS ARE TWO ORDERED ONE-SHOT JOBS: formbricks-migrate then hub-migrate; the app runs with SKIP_STARTUP_MIGRATION=true."

  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE: tarball is docker-compose.yml + cube/cube.js + cube/schema/FeedbackRecords.js."
  - "delete_deployment LEAVES THE MANAGED DATABASE BEHIND and it keeps billing; call delete_database to remove data."

Formbricks v5 baseline stack on one VM with managed Postgres beside it.
Five services plus two one-shot migration jobs; bundled Postgres replaced by redu managed Postgres.
About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month. Does not fit the no-card free trial.

content.text:
Everything is staged. Here's the plan — **nothing has been created yet.**

## Formbricks 5.3.4 on redu

| Resource | Size | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| App VM (`m1.mem16`, 4 vCPU / 16 GB) | 6 containers on one VM | GBP 0.0556/hr → 40.59/mo |
| Managed Postgres (`m1.small`, 1 vCPU / 2 GB) | own private VM, `pgvector` pre-installed | GBP 0.0174/hr → 12.70/mo |
| **Total** | | **GBP 0.073/hr ≈ GBP 53.29/mo** |

⛔ **Not covered by the no-card free trial** — the trial ceiling is m1.medium + one m1.small database. This needs a card. Note `m1.large` would be a *downgrade* here (8 GB vs 16 GB) for barely less money, so the flavor is passed explicitly.

**What goes up:** Formbricks web (pinned 5.3.4) + Hub (0.8.4) + Cube (v1.6.6) + Valkey (by digest), plus two ordered one-shot migration jobs. Public hostname pinned up front as **`formbricks-6w9jmneu.redu.cloud`** and wired into `WEBAPP_URL`/`NEXTAUTH_URL` before boot.

**Traps already handled:** bundled Postgres removed with all its `depends_on` entries · `HUB_DATABASE_URL` left unset (a second DB is refused at auth, SQLSTATE 28000) · Cube's two config files fetched into the tarball (missing = permanent 502) · Valkey's host `ports:` block deleted · named volume for the SAML path · GPU/taxonomy profiles off. I also corrected one thing against the source: `ENCRYPTION_KEY` is parsed as **hex unless it's exactly 32 chars** (`crypto.ts:10`), so it's a 64-char hex value, not a generic alphanumeric string.

⛔ **Be ready for one manual step the moment it's live:** the first person to load `/setup/signup` becomes administrator of the whole instance, and it's unauthenticated by design. It's a Next.js server action, so it can't be scripted with curl — you'll need to claim it in a browser immediately. I'll hand you the URL and then verify the door is shut.

**Licence:** the part you'll run is AGPL-3.0 (with `apps/web/modules/ee` under Formbricks' enterprise licence and the SDKs MIT). AGPL §13 puts a source-offer obligation on whoever *operates* the service over a network — that's you, not redu. Running the unmodified official image for your own org is the easy case; if you modify it and let others use it over the network, you owe them the modified source.

content.text:
The deploy **failed**, and the log gives an exact root cause. Let me diagnose before doing anything else.

`hub-migrate` ran migrations 001–003 fine, then died on 004:

```
004_add_feedback_records_embedding.sql: CREATE TABLE embeddings (... embedding halfvec(768) ...)
ERROR: type "halfvec" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42704)
```

`formbricks-migrate` exited **0** — Prisma's schema applied cleanly. Only Hub's goose chain broke, and `halfvec` is a **pgvector ≥ 0.7.0** type. So pgvector is genuinely required here (the recipe called it an unverified precaution — it isn't), and either the extension didn't get created or it's an older version. Let me look at the actual database.

content.text:
Root cause confirmed precisely:

- pgvector **is** installed (my `db_extensions: ['pgvector']` worked) — but it's **version 0.6.0**
- `halfvec` was introduced in pgvector **0.7.0**
- The DB VM's apt only offers 0.6.0 (`default_version 0.6.0`), on PostgreSQL 16.14

So this isn't a missing extension, it's a *too-old* one. Hub's migration 004 is mandatory in the goose chain, so there's no way around it — pgvector needs upgrading on the database VM. Let me check what's obtainable.

content.text:
Health monitor stopped (it would have polled a dead stack for an hour).

## Where things stand

The deploy failed with a **new gotcha the recipe doesn't know about**, and I've diagnosed it to the exact line:

| | |
|---|---|
| `formbricks-migrate` | ✅ exited 0 — Prisma schema applied |
| `hub-migrate` 001–003 | ✅ applied |
| `hub-migrate` **004** | ❌ `type "halfvec" does not exist` (SQLSTATE 42704) |
| Valkey | ✅ healthy |
| Cube / Hub / web | never started — gated behind the failed migration |

**Root cause:** redu's managed Postgres installs pgvector **0.6.0** (that's all Ubuntu noble's repo carries). `halfvec` arrived in pgvector **0.7.0**. So `db_extensions: ['pgvector']` did work — the extension is present, it's just three minor versions too old for Hub's embeddings migration. The recipe records pgvector as an unverified precaution; it's actually **required, at ≥ 0.7.0**.

I tried to build pgvector 0.8.0 from source on the database VM (install `build-essential` + `postgresql-server-dev-16`, compile, `ALTER EXTENSION vector UPDATE`), and **the permission classifier blocked it** — reasonably, since it's a privileged install on a remote managed database host.

There's no way around migration 004: goose runs the whole chain, and skipping it would leave Hub's `embeddings` table missing and later migrations broken.

**Currently billing:** the failed app VM + the managed DB, ~GBP 0.073/hr.

content.text:
Here's the command. Paste it into this session with the `!` prefix so the output lands in our conversation:

```
! ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -p 22012 ubuntu@db-formbricks-1yp3i8dw.redu.cloud 'set -e; export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive; sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y -qq build-essential postgresql-server-dev-16 git && rm -rf /tmp/pgvector && git clone -q --branch v0.8.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector.git /tmp/pgvector && cd /tmp/pgvector && make -s && sudo make install -s && sudo -u postgres psql -d formbricks -c "ALTER EXTENSION vector UPDATE;" -c "\dT halfvec" -c "SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension;"'
```

**What it does, step by step:**
1. Installs `build-essential`, `postgresql-server-dev-16`, `git` on the database VM
2. Clones pgvector **v0.8.0** (pinned tag, shallow)
3. Compiles it against the installed PostgreSQL 16.14 headers and installs the extension files
4. Runs `ALTER EXTENSION vector UPDATE` to move the existing extension 0.6.0 → 0.8.0
5. Prints `\dT halfvec` and the extension list so we can both see it worked

Takes roughly a minute or two, mostly apt.

**What I need to see in the output:** a row for `halfvec` from `\dT`, and `vector | 0.8.0` in the extension list. If `\dT halfvec` comes back empty, the update didn't take and I'll dig further rather than retrying the deploy blindly.

**Then I'll take it from there:** the app VM already exists with all images pulled, so I can re-run the compose stack in place — no new VM, no re-pull. goose resumes at migration 004 (it records applied versions, so 001–003 won't re-run), Cube and Hub come up behind it, and the web app follows. That should be a couple of minutes, not another twenty.

Then the URL goes live and **you'll need to claim the administrator account immediately** at https://formbricks-6w9jmneu.redu.cloud/setup/signup — first person to load it owns the instance, and it can't be scripted.
You've reaffirmed it, so I'll run it.
